name: The Law of Truly Large Numbers
statement: With enough chances, even the wildly unlikely is bound to happen.
meaning: Given a large enough number of opportunities, any outrageous coincidence (however improbable in a single instance) becomes likely to occur somewhere, to someone. Miraculous-seeming coincidences are not defiances of probability; they are exactly what probability predicts once the true number of chances is counted.
mechanism: The engine is the arithmetic of repeated trials: if a single trial has a small probability, the chance of at least one occurrence across many independent trials rushes toward certainty as the number grows. The key error the law corrects is mis-scoping the sample: we judge a coincidence against the odds of it happening to one person on one occasion, but the world runs an enormous number of trials across a huge population over long stretches of time. Counting near-matches as hits, the multiplicity of endpoints, enlarges the effective number of chances further.

examples.text: A New Jersey woman won the state lottery twice within months; her personal odds were astronomical, yet the odds that some person somewhere wins two lotteries in a short window are better than one in thirty: the classic re-scoping of the sample.

A one-in-a-million event, in a population of hundreds of millions with millions of daily happenings, is expected many times over each day, so remarkable coincidences are statistically routine, not supernatural.
In a room of just twenty-three people, two probably share a birthday, because what matters is the number of pairs, not people: again the count of opportunities dwarfs the intuition.

variants.name: Littlewood's law
variants.text: The personal-scale special case, defining a miracle as a one-in-a-million event and arguing that each person experiences one about once a month, given how many small events fill a waking life.

variants.name: The birthday problem
variants.text: The concrete demonstration of the same intuition, where the surprisingly high chance of a shared birthday comes from the large number of pairs among even a small group.

whyItMatters: It is the statistical antidote to belief in the miraculous, explaining why astonishing coincidences are expected rather than meaningful. It disciplines how we interpret rare events, prophetic-seeming dreams, and lucky streaks, and it is a staple of skeptical inquiry into the paranormal.

working.text: before marvelling at a coincidence, ask how many opportunities for it existed across all people, times, and near-matches, not just your own.
shift the question from the odds of this happening to you to the odds of something like it happening to someone, which is often near-certain.

working.lead: Do not read meaning into the rare
working.text: treat an expected coincidence as evidence of large numbers, not of a hidden cause or design.

limits: It is a colloquial principle about coincidences, not a formal theorem: it rests on the sound elementary probability that at least one occurrence becomes near-certain over enough trials. It must not be confused with the actual law of large numbers, a rigorously proven theorem about averages converging; the shared wording is a deliberate pun. It assumes the events are roughly independent with roughly constant probability, and it explains the base rate of coincidences without, by itself, ruling out a genuine cause in any particular case.
misreadings: It is not the law of large numbers, which is a proven theorem about sample averages converging to the expected value: the two share a name only as a pun. And it does not prove any specific coincidence is meaningless; it shows that coincidences in general are expected, so the burden is on claiming one is special.
origin: Named and formalised by Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller in 'Methods for Studying Coincidences,' Journal of the American Statistical Association 84(408):853-861 (1989), as a deliberate play on the law of large numbers.

sources.text: Diaconis, P. & Mosteller, F. (1989). “Methods for Studying Coincidences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, vol. 84. — the paper naming the law.
